name: Sticky Garlic Gochujang Chicken
why: Introduces the Chinese velveting technique — a game-changing method for ultra-tender, crispy chicken that's perfect for Korean-inspired weeknight dinners. Summer gochujang is trending, and this delivers sweet, spicy, garlicky flavor in 30 minutes.
author: Henry
ingredients: 1¼ lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts (or thighs/tenders), cut into ¾-inch pieces
2 tbsp gochujang paste (Korean red chili paste)

steps: In a bowl, combine 1 tbsp water, baking soda, kosher salt, sugar, white pepper, sesame oil, and 1 tbsp soy sauce. Stir until baking soda dissolves.
Add the chicken pieces, stir to coat, and let sit for 10 minutes. The baking soda tenderizes the meat — this is the velveting technique.
Add cornstarch to the bowl with the chicken and stir until all pieces are evenly coated. This creates the crispy exterior when fried.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the remaining 2 tbsp soy sauce, honey, gochujang paste, and rice vinegar until smooth.
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a deep skillet over medium-high heat.
Add half the chicken in a single layer and cook undisturbed for 2-3 minutes until golden brown on one side.
Flip and cook another 2-4 minutes until golden and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Add more oil if needed and repeat with the remaining chicken.
Lower skillet heat to medium-low and let the pan cool for 2 minutes.
Add a small drizzle of oil and sauté the minced garlic until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Increase heat to high. Pour in the sauce and let it sizzle and bubble for 30 seconds.
Add the fried chicken back to the skillet and toss until every piece is evenly coated in the sticky glaze. Remove from heat.
Top with sliced green onions and toasted sesame seeds.
Serve immediately over fluffy steamed rice with your favorite steamed vegetables.

pro_tips: The velveting technique (baking soda + resting) is the secret to restaurant-quality tender chicken — it breaks down proteins so the meat stays juicy even when fried at high heat. Works with any protein.
Adjust gochujang to your heat preference: 1 tbsp for mild, 2 tbsp for medium, 3 tbsp for spicy. Martin's spice profile suggests 2 tbsp is the sweet spot for aromatic dishes.
